Hadron. Hadrons are composite particles made of quarks bound by gluon exchange through the strong nuclear force. The two primary hadron classes are baryons—three quarks—and mesons—quark-antiquark pairs. All hadrons are color-neutral and confined. Individual quarks cannot escape. The proton and neutron are the most stable and abundant hadrons.

Hadrons are composite structures of quarks and gluons called partons. Color confinement is fundamental: only color-neutral combinations form hadrons. Red quarks must pair with antired, green with antigreen, and blue with antiblue. The two main categories of hadrons are baryons, which contain three quarks and carry baryon number plus one, and mesons, which contain one quark-antiquark pair and carry baryon number zero. Hadrons interact via all four fundamental forces, though the strong force dominates their internal structure. Most hadrons are unstable and decay within picoseconds or less. The hadron spectrum contains hundreds of resonances, with patterns explained by the quark model. Internal structure can be probed via deep inelastic scattering, which reveals parton distributions within hadrons.

Hadrons are the only form in which quarks are observed in nature. Single quarks cannot be isolated. The proton, composed of two up quarks and one down quark, is the universe's most abundant baryon. Hadron phenomenology drives modern particle physics: rare hadron decays constrain physics beyond the Standard Model, and the quark-gluon plasma—a hadron-dissolving state—existed microseconds after the Big Bang.
